Empirical Research Plan:  U.S. Wheat Food-Aid Shipments and Armed Conflict, 1972–2006

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
Strategy: Two-stage least squares (shift–share instrumental variables) implemented in a country-year panel with country and year fixed effects, complemented by an event-study on the reduced form.

Why IV? 
• Food-aid deliveries are clearly endogenous: the U.S. deliberately targets needy or geopolitically strategic countries, and conflict risk itself can trigger shipments.  
• Large, plausibly exogenous shocks to the *supply* of U.S. wheat arise from weather-driven production fluctuations inside the United States. Because PL-480 wheat is shipped the year after harvest, lagged U.S. production affects the *quantity* of wheat available for aid but is orthogonal to contemporaneous political conditions in recipient countries.  
• Countries differ sharply in their historical propensity to receive U.S. wheat.  Multiplying the common shock (lagged U.S. wheat production) by a time-invariant country-specific share generates a powerful shift–share instrument that varies by country and year.

Formally:
1st stage:  FoodAid_it = π · (Z_it) + ϕ_i + λ_t + X_it β + u_it  
2nd stage:  Conflict_it = β · FoodAid_it + ϕ_i + λ_t + X_it γ + ε_it  
where Z_it = Elig_i × U.S.WheatProd_{t–1}

An event-study on the reduced form (Conflict_it on Z_it with distributed leads/lags) will probe parallel-trends style pre-period dynamics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control

Treatment variable
• FoodAid_it = log(1 + thousand metric tons of U.S. wheat shipped to country i in year t).

Instrument construction
• Elig_i = average share of global U.S. wheat food-aid tonnage that country i received during a pre-period (1957-1971). This is time-invariant.  
• Shock_t = (log) U.S. wheat production in harvest year t–1 (USDA).  
• Z_it = Elig_i × Shock_t.

Control group / counterfactual
• The 134 non-OECD countries when they *happen* to receive less or zero wheat aid, leveraged through the cross-country heterogeneity in Elig_i and the year-to-year exogenous variation in Shock_t. Countries with Elig_i ≈ 0 act as “always controls” in years when U.S. production is high.

Timing
• Treatment year t corresponds to wheat harvested in the U.S. in year t–1 and generally shipped/arriving the same calendar year t.

No running variable or cutoff (RDD not used).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions

A1 – Instrument relevance:  Lagged U.S. wheat production strongly predicts the quantity of wheat shipped abroad, *conditional on* eligibilities.  (Plausible; historically large surpluses translate mechanically into PL-480 outflows.)

A2 – Exclusion restriction:  Conditional on controls, country and year fixed effects, and recipient-year weather & economic covariates, lagged U.S. wheat production affects recipient-country conflict only through food-aid deliveries.  (Plausible because the U.S. share of world wheat supply is large but its *production shocks* mainly shift domestic stocks and aid quantities, not international prices; we will still control for world wheat price.)

A3 – Time-invariant eligibilities are exogenous with respect to *contemporaneous* conflict shocks.  (Elig_i is based on a pre-sample window; plausibility high, though historical geopolitics could correlate—addressed in threats section.)

A4 – No spillovers (SUTVA): An increase in food aid to country i does not materially alter conflict risk in country j, conditional on year FE.  (Potentially violated in contiguous famine zones; we will test by excluding neighbors.)

A5 – Monotonicity: Higher U.S. wheat production never *reduces* shipments to high-eligibility countries (no “defiers”).  (Institutionally reasonable.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigating Actions

Threat 1:  Global wheat prices and recipient food security move with U.S. production, violating exclusion.  
• Mitigation: Control for log world wheat price, recipient cereal production, precipitation, temperature, and their lags; show results are robust to adding those controls. Use *state-level* U.S. weather shocks (e.g., degree-days in Great Plains) aggregated with fixed weights as an alternative shock that is orthogonal to world prices.

Threat 2:  Historical eligibility (Elig_i) may be correlated with unobserved, time-invariant propensity for conflict (e.g., strategic allies).  
• Mitigation: Country fixed effects already partial out level differences; nonetheless, re-estimate after interacting year trends with (i) continent and (ii) baseline polity score categories to allow for differential evolution; re-weight sample using entropy balancing on covariates correlated with Elig_i.

Threat 3:  Measurement error or anticipatory behavior (armed groups learn about incoming aid).  
• Mitigation: (i) Use multiple sources (FAOSTAT, USAID) for aid quantities; (ii) re-specify using *t + 1* conflict outcomes to allow for lagged effects; (iii) event-study to verify no pre-trends up to 3 years before large aid shocks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)

```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)     # fast FE and IV
library(lmtest)     # for coeftest
library(sandwich)   # robust vcov

# ---- 1. Data loading ----
# Assume CSV files are in working directory
aid   <- read_csv("wheat_aid.csv")        # country, year, wheat_tmt
prod  <- read_csv("us_wheat_production.csv") # year, us_prod
conf  <- read_csv("conflict_prio.csv")    # country, year, civil_any25, civil_1000, interstate25
weather <- read_csv("recipient_weather.csv") # country, year, temp, precip
controls <- read_csv("controls.csv")      # GDPpc, polity, road_density, etc.

# ---- 2. Merge and construct variables ----
df <- aid %>% 
  full_join(prod,  by = "year") %>% 
  full_join(conf,  by = c("country","year")) %>% 
  full_join(weather,by = c("country","year")) %>% 
  full_join(controls,by = c("country","year")) %>%
  arrange(country, year)

# Create historical eligibility (using 1957-1971)
eligibility <- df %>% 
  filter(year >= 1957 & year <= 1971) %>% 
  group_by(country) %>% 
  summarise(Elig = sum(wheat_tmt, na.rm = TRUE) / 
                  sum(df$wheat_tmt[df$year>=1957 & df$year<=1971], na.rm = TRUE))

df <- left_join(df, eligibility, by = "country")

# Treatment and instrument
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(l_wheatAid = log1p(wheat_tmt),
         us_prod_lag = lag(us_prod, 1),
         Shock       = log(us_prod_lag + 1),
         Z           = Elig * Shock)

# ---- 3. Main IV regression ----
main_iv <- feols(civil_any25 ~ l_wheatAid | 
                   country + year | 
                   (l_wheatAid ~ Z),
                 data = df, cluster = "country")
summary(main_iv)

# ---- 4. Event-study (reduced form) ----
df <- df %>% 
  group_by(country) %>% 
  mutate(Z_lead1 = lead(Z,1), Z_lead2 = lead(Z,2),
         Z_lag1  = lag(Z,1),  Z_lag2 = lag(Z,2))

event <- feols(civil_any25 ~ Z + Z_lag1 + Z_lag2 + Z_lead1 + Z_lead2 |
                 country + year,
               data = df, cluster = "country")
summary(event)

# ---- 5. Robustness: exclude top-eligibility outliers ----
df_rb <- df %>% filter(Elig < quantile(Elig, .99, na.rm=TRUE))
rb_iv <- feols(civil_any25 ~ l_wheatAid | country + year | 
                 (l_wheatAid ~ Z),
               data = df_rb, cluster = "country")
etable(main_iv, rb_iv, tex = FALSE)
```

(Adjust variable names as needed; `civil_any25` is the indicator for intra-state conflict ≥ 25 deaths.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results (Prior)

Theoretical mechanisms suggest *both* violence-decreasing (consumption smoothing, lower food prices) and violence-increasing (looting, financing of militias) channels. Given the documented ease with which wheat shipments can be expropriated in weak states, my prior is a net *positive* effect on conflict:

• A one-standard-deviation increase in shipments (~20,000 t; ≈ 2 log pts) will raise the probability of a civil conflict onset by ≈ 1-2 percentage points from a baseline of ~12 %.  
• Effects will be concentrated in civil (not interstate) wars, larger in ethnically fractionalized and low-road-density countries, and stronger for minor conflicts (25-999 deaths) than major wars.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)

C1 – Instrument relevance (1 = satisfied): 1  (Expect first-stage F > 15).  
C2 – Exclusion restriction plausible: 0.5  (Some concern via world prices).  
C3 – Monotonicity / no defiers: 1.  
C4 – SUTVA / no spillovers: 0.5  (Country spillovers possible).  
C5 – No differential trends correlated with Elig_i: 0.5  (Addressed with interactions).

Total: 3.5 / 5 (credible but must be demonstrated empirically).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan outlines a transparent, testable strategy exploiting plausibly exogenous variation in U.S. wheat surpluses to identify the causal impact of food aid on armed conflict across recipient countries.
